places.name: SHIV SHAKTI POINT — Chandrayaan-3 landing site
places.blurb: Where Vikram set down in August 2023, on undulating mare-highland regolith south of 69 S. The ground is not steep; it is simply never the same twice.

places.name: SHACKLETON RIM — the lunar south pole
places.blurb: A real 13 degree rim grade, from LOLA polar topography at 5 m/px — the finest lunar terrain published anywhere. Steep enough that the ankle runs out of dorsiflexion before the solver runs out of ideas.

places.name: MARE TRANQUILLITATIS — flat basalt plain
places.blurb: The flattest window the terrain scan could find, which is the point: with nothing to negotiate, the only thing left to compare is efficiency.

places.name: ARISTARCHUS — blocky ejecta and scarps
places.blurb: The brightest region on the Moon, and the roughest ground in this set. The problem here is obstacle GEOMETRY rather than grade.

places.name: TYCHO FLANK — steep downhill braking
places.blurb: Down a 13.6 degree flank of young Tycho ejecta. Downhill at one sixth g is a braking problem: there is little weight to brake with and a very long time to fall.

places.name: SCHRÖDINGER BASIN — mixed terrain
places.blurb: A 320 km farside impact basin with a volcanic vent on its floor. Cruise, rough walking and a climb in one traverse.

places.name: JEZERO CRATER — the western delta front
places.blurb: Where Perseverance landed in February 2021, at the front of a river delta that emptied into a crater lake. Cobbles and boulders shed from the scarp.

places.name: GALE CRATER — lower Mount Sharp
places.blurb: Curiosity's ground, read from the 1 m/px HiRISE mosaic — the finest DEM of anywhere on Mars, and the only site here whose landforms are resolved at the scale a robot walks.

places.name: OLYMPIA UNDAE — north polar dune sea
places.blurb: The largest dune field on Mars, wrapped around the north polar cap. Deep sand: the DEM gives the regional grade and the ripple the foot sinks into is synthesised.

places.name: CERBERUS FOSSAE — fissure system
places.blurb: Young tectonic fissures, and the source of most of the marsquakes InSight recorded. The fissure is narrower than a 200 m pixel, so the DEM supplies the plain it cuts and nothing more.

places.name: MEDUSAE FOSSAE — yardang field
places.blurb: The largest deposit of loose material on Mars, carved by wind into parallel ridges. Threading between yardangs, all of them running the same way.

places.name: GANGES CHASMA — Valles Marineris wall
places.blurb: The steepest wall section the terrain scan could find in the eastern Valles Marineris. Descent by switchback, on talus.

places.name: DESTINY — the US laboratory
places.blurb: The US laboratory, and the module with the most rack-mounted equipment to collide with. Twenty-four rack bays, so the free corridor down the middle is narrower than the shell suggests.

places.name: HARMONY — Node 2
places.blurb: The forward node: six berthing ports, so it is the busiest junction on the station and the one where a push in the wrong axis has the most ways to end badly.

places.name: COLUMBUS — ESA laboratory
places.blurb: The ESA laboratory. Short and wide, which makes it the hardest module to cross without touching anything: there is less distance to bleed off a bad push in.

places.name: KIBO — Japanese Experiment Module
places.blurb: The largest single module on the station, and the one the crews use to demonstrate free flight because it is the only place with room to get a clean run at it.

places.name: UNITY — Node 1
places.blurb: The first US node, and the oldest American element in orbit. Short, with hatches on all six faces.

places.name: TRANQUILITY — Node 3
places.blurb: Node 3, which carries the exercise equipment and the life support. Where the crew spend the most time deliberately loading their legs.

places.name: ZVEZDA — service module
places.blurb: The Russian service module and the station's original core: crew quarters, galley, and the longest single run on the station.

places.name: CUPOLA — the observation module
places.blurb: Seven windows and almost no length at all. There is not enough room here to push off and glide; the whole scenario becomes arriving and stopping.

microScenes.name: MOMENTUM GAP — is there enough push to arrive?
microScenes.blurb: Both robots push off the same wall. WorldVLA leaves with 0.18 m/s and, finding itself short, swims — a full breaststroke that cannot work, because with no external contact the centre of mass keeps exactly the velocity the wall gave it. Every sweep of the arms only rocks the body about a COM that will not move. PragyaSpace computes the impulse the gap requires, leaves at 0.42 m/s and coasts to the rail.

microScenes.name: BRAKE GAP — can the momentum be removed on arrival?
microScenes.blurb: Identical 0.72 m/s departures, 25.2 N s of momentum to shed. PragyaSpace positions the lead hand early, catches the rail at 4.8 s and lets the elbow and shoulder absorb the arrest over a quarter second. WorldVLA reaches late, misses the capture and takes the impulse from the bulkhead instead.
